'''Johnson:''' {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} {{legend0|#584cde|70–80%}} {{legend0|#3933e5|80–90%}}
'''Pressler:''' {{legend0|#e27f7f|50–60%}} {{legend0|#d75d5d|60–70%}} {{legend0|#d72f30|70–80%}} | title = U.S. Senator | before_election = [[Larry Pressler]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Tim Johnson (South Dakota politician)|Tim Johnson]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{ElectionsSD}} The '''1996 United States Senate election in South Dakota''' was held on November 5, 1996. Incumbent Republican Senator [[Larry Pressler]] lost his bid for a fourth term to Democratic nominee [[Tim Johnson (South Dakota politician)|Tim Johnson]] by 8,579 votes and a 2.64% margin. Pressler was the only incumbent U.S. Senator to lose a general election in the [[1996 United States elections|1996 election]] cycle, of which this was the only Democratic flip.{{Cite web |date=2004-11-16 |title=AllPolitics - South Dakota Senate Race - Nov. 6, 1996 |website=[[CNN]] |url=http://www.cnn.com/ALLPOLITICS/1996/news/9611/05/senate/sd/ |access-date=2023-08-15 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20041116213158/http://www.cnn.com/ALLPOLITICS/1996/news/9611/05/senate/sd/ |archive-date=November 16, 2004 }}{{Cite web |last=Barrett |first=R. Morris |date=1996-11-06 |title=AllPolitics - A Status Quo Senate - Nov. 6, 1996 |url=http://www.cnn.com/ALLPOLITICS/1996/news/9611/05/senate/analysis/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20011005230314/http://www.cnn.com/ALLPOLITICS/1996/news/9611/05/senate/analysis/ |archive-date=2001-10-05 |access-date=2023-08-30 |website=www.cnn.com}} He later ran again unsuccessfully for this seat as an Independent in [[2014 United States Senate election in South Dakota|2014]], when Johnson did not seek re-election. == General election == === Candidates === * [[Tim Johnson (South Dakota politician)|Tim Johnson]], U.S. Representative at-large (Democratic) * [[Larry Pressler]], incumbent U.S. Senator (Republican) === Campaign === The race between Larry Pressler and Tim Johnson was one of the most competitive Senate races that year. From the onset, Johnson was seen as a potential candidate,{{Cite book |last=Curran |first=Tim |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qlkeAAAAIBAJ&dq=larry+pressler+tim+johnson+primary+opposition&pg=PA15&article_id=2083,3082733 |title=GOP licking chops over '96 prospects |publisher=Times Daily |date=1994-11-20 |pages=D1 |language=en}} and it was thought Pressler would face a tough race were Johnson, the state's sole congressman since 1987, to enter.{{Cite book |last=Brasher |first=Phillip |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qo8xAAAAIBAJ&dq=pressler+johnson+1996&pg=PA19&article_id=2686,8223602 |title=Phone PACS aids bill's sponsor |publisher=Rome News-Tribune |date=1995-08-06 |pages=2E |language=en}} Initially Johnson was quiet on his 1996 plans{{Cite web |last=Lawrence |first=Tom |date=2014-12-16 |title=Lawrence: Tim Johnson's graceful exit from the Senate |url=https://www.aberdeennews.com/story/opinion/2014/12/16/lawrence-tim-johnsons-graceful-exit-from-the-senate/45409433/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230829222201/https://www.aberdeennews.com/story/opinion/2014/12/16/lawrence-tim-johnsons-graceful-exit-from-the-senate/45409433/ |archive-date=2023-08-29 |access-date=2023-08-29 |website=Aberdeen News |language=en-US}} but after a delay due to his wife's breast cancer surgery,{{Cite book |last=Espo |first=David |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PGlGAAAAIBAJ&dq=larry+pressler+tim+johnson+primary&pg=PA3&article_id=1326,859070 |title=Democrats grow optimistic over Senate races |publisher=The Daily Gazette |date=1996-03-04 |pages=A5 |language=en}} Johnson formally entered the race on April 2, 1996.{{Cite news |last=Kranz |first=David |date=1996-04-03 |title=Johnson says he'll fight for S.D. values in Senate |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/argus-leader-johnson-says-hell-fight-fo/142328799/ |access-date=2024-02-28 |work=Argus-Leader |pages=1}} Neither candidate faced any primary opposition.{{Cite news |last=Rosenbaum |first=David E. |date=1996-10-19 |title=A Rare Sighting in South Dakota: An Incumbent in a Battle for Re-election |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1996/10/19/us/a-rare-sighting-in-south-dakota-an-incumbent-in-a-battle-for-re-election.html |url-status=live |access-date=2023-08-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131113062235/https://www.nytimes.com/1996/10/19/us/a-rare-sighting-in-south-dakota-an-incumbent-in-a-battle-for-re-election.html |archive-date=2013-11-13 |issn=0362-4331}} One of the biggest issues of this campaign had to do with Pressler, the chair of the [[United States Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation|Senate Commerce Committee]], and his increased stature. For example, Pressler received criticism for his suggestions to privatize public television.{{Cite news |last1=Anderson |first1=Jack |last2=Binstein |first2=Michael |date=2023-08-29 |title=PRESSLER AND THE BARNEY' BACKLASH - The Washington Post |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1995/02/13/pressler-and-the-barney-backlash/29e7c7b2-9c7c-47bd-af4e-a8611dc11e5c/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230829230400/https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1995/02/13/pressler-and-the-barney-backlash/29e7c7b2-9c7c-47bd-af4e-a8611dc11e5c/ |archive-date=2023-08-29 |access-date=2023-08-29 |newspaper=Washington Post}} He also faced criticism for enquiring the ethnic background and gender identity of [[PBS]] employees.{{Cite news |last=Witt |first=Karen de |date=1995-02-03 |title=Queries on Public Radio Staff Start Furor |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1995/02/03/us/queries-on-public-radio-staff-start-furor.html |url-status=live |access-date=2023-08-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150526141548/https://www.nytimes.com/1995/02/03/us/queries-on-public-radio-staff-start-furor.html |archive-date=2015-05-26 |issn=0362-4331}} The backlash from the situation also led to bumper stickers saying "Keep public TV, privatize Pressler" popping up around the state.{{Cite news |last=Marks |first=Alexandra |date=1995-09-20 |title=PBS Is Bowed But Unbroken In Budget Battle |work=Christian Science Monitor |url=https://www.csmonitor.com/1995/0920/20013.html |url-status=live |access-date=2023-08-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150926181142/https://www.csmonitor.com/1995/0920/20013.html |archive-date=2015-09-26 |issn=0882-7729}} Another issue which would arise was related to the [[Telecommunications Act of 1996]] a bill which Pressler authored.{{Cite book |last=Shribman |first=David |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QTczAAAAIBAJ&dq=larry+pressler+chair+of+commerce&pg=PA8&article_id=2868,4226621 |title=Contentious Senate Campaign in South Dakota |publisher=Lawrence Journal-World |date=1996-09-23 |pages=6B |language=en}} Johnson used the bill to attack Pressler for rising phone prices in South Dakota. This especially became a problem when Pressler had to pull an ad claiming phone rates went down, even though they had not. More challenging for Pressler, however, were the attacks relating to PAC donations Pressler received. Pressler received significant donations from telecommunication entities and their [[Political action committee|Political Action Committees]]. In the first nine months of 1995, Pressler received more PAC donations than any other politician.{{Cite book |last=L'Hommedieu |first=Jon |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3hoOAAAAIBAJ&dq=larry+pressler+1995&pg=PA3&article_id=2055,3855006 |title='Clean up Congress' means getting rid of PAC funds |publisher=The Daily Courier |date=1996-05-29 |pages=4A |language=en}}{{Cite news |date=2023-08-29 |title=Washingtonpost.com: Contributions On Call |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-srv/politics/special/oncall/stories/oc092196.htm |access-date=2023-08-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230829233304/https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-srv/politics/special/oncall/stories/oc092196.htm |archive-date=August 29, 2023 }} In a small state such as South Dakota, this meant the money could be spent on numerous ads. That said, this proved a double edged sword for Pressler. Johnson criticized Pressler for the donations he took from these companies and tied the donations to the Telecom bill.{{Cite book |last=Schantz |first=Harvey L. |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.4324/9780203903155 |title=Politics in an Era of Divided Government |date=2013-05-13 |publisher=Routledge |doi=10.4324/9780203903155 |isbn=978-1-135-57766-7}} Similarly, on tobacco donations, Pressler faced criticism for accepting over $50,000 in money from the tobacco industry, whereas Johnson had stopped accepting donations in 1995.{{Cite web |last=Neergaard |first=Lauran |date=1996-09-05 |title=NEWSPAPER ADS SUPPORT FDA'S TOBACCO CRACKDOWN |url=https://greensboro.com/newspaper-ads-support-fdas-tobacco-crackdown/article_4a29c5f2-0067-5fab-96d8-b28e46c4f9c3.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230829235325/https://greensboro.com/article_4a29c5f2-0067-5fab-96d8-b28e46c4f9c3.html |archive-date=2023-08-29 |access-date=2023-08-29 |website=Greensboro News and Record |language=en}} This, coupled with allegations of Pressler using campaign funds for lavish travel, fed into Johnson's attacks that Pressler lost touch with the state's voters.{{Cite book |last=Associated Press |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=IzEjAAAAIBAJ&dq=pressler+johnson+1996&pg=PA3&article_id=5099,5997653 |title=South Dakota senator in peril of losing seat |publisher=The Southeast Missourian |date=1996-09-23 |pages=4A |language=en}}{{Cite news |last=Dewar |first=Helen |date=1996-10-20 |title=NO MORE MR. NICE GUYS IN SOUTH DAKOTA |language=en-US |newspaper=Washington Post |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/politics/1996/10/20/no-more-mr-nice-guys-in-south-dakota/3d6b6b9f-c8cd-4a08-b6d1-d990c30c576d/ |url-status=live |access-date=2023-08-30 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170828204646/https://www.washingtonpost.com/web/20170828204646/https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/politics/1996/10/20/no-more-mr-nice-guys-in-south-dakota/3d6b6b9f-c8cd-4a08-b6d1-d990c30c576d/?utm_term=.d1526755ea98 |archive-date=2017-08-28 |issn=0190-8286}} Johnson had faced the advantage of being the states lone U.S. House member, which some believe put him on an even keel with Pressler, and created the dynamic of an incumbent against another incumbent. Johnson also had a better record of winning, never getting less than 59% of the vote in his five campaigns and over performing Pressler on the same ballot in 1990.{{Cite book |last=Lowy |first=Joan |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=v2UlAAAAIBAJ&dq=larry+pressler+tim+johnson+primary&pg=PA11&article_id=1037,6575946 |title=Control of the Senate appears too close to call |publisher=Reading Eagle |date=1996-10-13 |pages=A20 |language=en}} Pressler tried to attack Johnson's record charging that he was too liberal for voters of South Dakota. Pressler ran numerous ads, starting in July 1995, attacking Johnson as a liberal, though Johnson's campaign's polling showed these attacks did not land.{{Cite book |last=Struble |first=Karl |title=Campaigns and elections: contemporary case studies |publisher=CQ press |year=2000 |isbn=978-1-56802-495-0 |location=Washington (D.C) |pages=67}} In terms of polling, it was seen as a close race throughout, albeit mostly through internal polls. In the end, Johnson was the victor of a close race, 166,533 votes (51%) to 157,954 votes (49%) in spite, of being outspent 8 to 5.{{Cite book |last1=Slavin |first1=Peter |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LfEvAAAAIBAJ&dq=larry+pressler+tim+johnson+1996&pg=PA9&article_id=3262,5373380 |title=Incumbency helps congressional candidates |last2=Gallman |first2=Vanessa |publisher=Lakeland Ledger |date=1996-11-05 |pages=A17 |language=en}} === Results === {{Election box begin | title = General election results{{cite web | url=https://sdsos.gov/elections-voting/election-resources/election-history/1996/1996_general_election_returns_presidential_statewide_candidates.aspx | title=Election Resources: South Dakota Secretary of State }}}} {{Election box winning candidate with party link | party = Democratic Party (United States) | candidate = [[Tim Johnson (South Dakota politician)|Tim Johnson]] | votes = 166,533 | percentage = 51.32% | change = +6.25% }} {{Election box candidate with party link | party = Republican Party (United States) | candidate = [[Larry Pressler]] (incumbent) | votes = 157,954 | percentage = 48.68% | change = -3.71% }} {{Election box total | votes = 324,487 | percentage = 100.00% | change = N/A }} {{Election box gain with party link no swing | winner = Democratic Party (United States) | loser = Republican Party (United States) | swing = }} {{Election box end}} ==See also== * [[1996 United States Senate elections]] ==References== {{Reflist}} {{United States elections, 1996}} [[Category:1996 United States Senate elections|South Dakota]] [[Category:United States Senate elections in South Dakota|1996]] [[Category:1996 elections in South Dakota]]
